questions.title: What intellectual property is
questions.text: What is **intellectual property**?

options.content: Any object a person buys, such as a laptop or a phone
Creations of the mind — inventions, software, texts, music, designs, logos — that the creator owns and has legal rights over
Information stored on a government server
The hardware of a computer system

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: IP is not a physical object: it is the creation itself, e.g. a program's code or a song.

questions.title: Copyright, patent or trademark
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show how each item is protected.

prefill: The source code of a mobile app
A new design of solar panel that produces more energy
The logo of a bank
A novel written by a student

scheme.mark_scheme: Source code → Copyright (1); Solar panel → Patent (1); Logo → Trademark (1); Novel → Copyright (1)

questions.title: Copyright or patent?
questions.text: Tick (✓) whether each statement describes **copyright** or a **patent**.

prefill: Arises automatically when the work is created
Protects a new invention, device or process
Must be applied for and registered
Protects the source code of a program
Lasts about 20 years

scheme.mark_scheme: Arises automatically when the work is created – Copyright (1); Protects a new invention, device or process – Patent (1); Must be applied for and registered – Patent (1); Protects the source code of a program – Copyright (1); Lasts about 20 years – Patent (1)

questions.title: Copyright is automatic
questions.text: A photo on a website is free for anyone to use because it is on the Internet.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: Copyright applies automatically; the photo can only be used with permission or under its licence.

questions.title: What a trademark protects
questions.text: A start-up registers the name and logo of its delivery app. Which protection is this?

options.content: Copyright
Patent
Trademark
Trade secret

scheme.mark_scheme: C
scheme.explanation: Brand names, logos and slogans are protected by a registered trademark (®).

questions.title: Software licences
questions.text: Match each type of licence to its description.

right.text: Must be paid for; copying and changing are not allowed
Free for a trial period, then must be paid for
Free to use, but the source code is not available
Free, and the source code can be studied and modified

scheme.mark_scheme: L1–R1, L2–R2, L3–R3, L4–R4. One mark per correct match.

questions.title: What each licence allows
questions.text: Tick (✓) the **only** licence type for which each statement is true.

prefill: The source code can be studied and modified
Free for a trial period, then must be paid for
Must be bought before use; copying is not allowed
Free to use, but the source code is not available

scheme.mark_scheme: The source code can be studied and modified – Open source (1); Free for a trial period, then must be paid for – Shareware (1); Must be bought before use; copying is not allowed – Proprietary (1); Free to use, but the source code is not available – Freeware (1)

questions.title: Creative Commons
questions.text: An image has the licence **CC BY-NC**. What may you do with it?

options.content: Sell it on T-shirts without credit
Use it in a school project with credit to the author
Claim it as your own work
Use it in a paid advertisement

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: BY = give credit to the author; NC = non-commercial use only.

questions.title: Effects of piracy
questions.text: People download pirated copies of a computer game made in Almaty. Select **three** consequences of this.

options.content: The developer loses income from sales
The game automatically becomes open source
Players of pirated copies risk malware and get no updates
The developer has less money to pay staff and make new games
The game's copyright ends
The players' computers run faster

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.
scheme.explanation: Analyse piracy by who is harmed: the creator (income, jobs), the user (malware, no support, fines) and society.

questions.title: Recognising plagiarism
questions.text: Which of these is **plagiarism**?

options.content: Quoting a sentence in quotation marks and citing the website
Copying paragraphs from a blog into an essay and presenting them as your own words
Using an open-source library according to its licence
Buying a licence for photo-editing software

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Plagiarism is presenting someone else's work or ideas as your own without acknowledging the source.

questions.title: Using an image legally
questions.text: Select **two** legal ways a student can use an image from the Internet on a school website.

options.content: Use an image with a Creative Commons licence and credit the author
Use any image found with a search engine because it is public
Ask the photographer for permission
Crop the image so nobody recognises it
Remove the watermark

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: A documentary for a competition
questions.text: Students make a video about Almaty for a competition. Match each item they want to use with the **correct** behaviour.

left.text: A popular song as background music
Photos found with a search engine
A paragraph from a travel website

right.text: Write it in their own words and cite the website
Buy a licence or use an open-source editor
Use royalty-free / Creative Commons music, or get permission
Use Creative Commons photos and credit each author

scheme.mark_scheme: A popular song as background music – Use royalty-free / Creative Commons music, or get permission; Photos found with a search engine – Use Creative Commons photos and credit each author; A paragraph from a travel website – Write it in their own words and cite the website; Video-editing software – Buy a licence or use an open-source editor.

questions.title: Problems caused by fake news
questions.text: A false post claims that a herbal tea cures flu, and it is shared thousands of times. Select **three** problems this can cause.

options.content: People may not see a doctor and become seriously ill
Trust in reliable sources such as doctors falls
The post becomes protected by a patent
People waste money on a product that does not work
Social media stops working

scheme.mark_scheme: A and B and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Checking online information
questions.text: Select **two** good ways to check whether information found online is reliable.

options.content: Check who published it and whether the author is known
Count the number of likes
Compare it with other reliable sources
Check that it has many exclamation marks
Trust it if a friend shared it

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Misinformation or disinformation
questions.text:
Complete the sentences.

False information spread by mistake is called [[1]]. False information spread deliberately to deceive is called [[2]]. Presenting someone else's work as your own is called [[3]].

scheme.mark_scheme: (1) misinformation (2) disinformation (3) plagiarism

questions.title: Disseminating information
questions.text: Select **two** actions that are problems caused by disseminating information without permission.

options.content: Posting a classmate's phone number and address on social media
Citing a website in a bibliography
Uploading a new film to a file-sharing site
Using an open-source library according to its licence

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Quoting for education
questions.text: Copyright law allows a student to quote a short part of a book in an essay without permission, as long as the source is acknowledged.

scheme.mark_scheme: True.
scheme.explanation: Exceptions (fair use) allow limited use for education, criticism, news and quotation with the source acknowledged.

questions.title: What e-government is
questions.text: What is **e-government**?

options.content: A social network for government officials
The use of the Internet and digital technologies by the state to provide public services online
An online shop that sells government products
Software that counts votes in elections only

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: In Kazakhstan the main portal is egov.kz with the eGov mobile app.

questions.title: The main portal
questions.text: State the web address of the main e-government portal of Kazakhstan.

scheme.mark_scheme: egov.kz

questions.title: Choosing a service
questions.text: Match each citizen's need to what they can do on eGov.

left.text: A parent wants a place for a child in kindergarten
A driver received a speeding fine
A graduate needs proof of no criminal record
A family moved to a new flat

right.text: Get a certificate of no criminal record
Register the new place of residence
Apply to a kindergarten online
Pay the fine online

scheme.mark_scheme: A parent wants a place for a child in kindergarten – Apply to a kindergarten online; A driver received a speeding fine – Pay the fine online; A graduate needs proof of no criminal record – Get a certificate of no criminal record; A family moved to a new flat – Register the new place of residence.

questions.title: Steps to receive a service
questions.text: Match each step number to the action when receiving a certificate on egov.kz.

right.text: Sign the request with the EDS or SMS code
Download the result from the personal account
Log in with an EDS or password + SMS code
Choose the service in the catalogue
Check the form filled in from state databases

scheme.mark_scheme: Step 1 – Log in with an EDS or password + SMS code; Step 2 – Choose the service in the catalogue; Step 3 – Check the form filled in from state databases; Step 4 – Sign the request with the EDS or SMS code; Step 5 – Download the result from the personal account.

questions.title: Why no paper copies are needed
questions.text: Why does a citizen usually **not** need to upload copies of documents when applying on egov.kz?

options.content: The portal does not check any data
The portal gets the data from state databases using the citizen's IIN
Officials visit the citizen at home
Paper documents are not legal in Kazakhstan

scheme.mark_scheme: B

questions.title: What an EDS proves
questions.text: Select **two** things that an electronic digital signature (EDS) proves about a signed document.

options.content: Who signed the document
That the document is free of spelling mistakes
That the document has not been changed after signing
That the document was printed
That the computer has antivirus software

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: What an EDS is
questions.text: An electronic digital signature is a scanned picture of a person's handwritten signature.

scheme.mark_scheme: False.
scheme.explanation: An EDS is a cryptographic key pair (private key + public certificate), not an image.

questions.title: Ways to log in
questions.text: Match each eGov login method to how it works.

right.text: Confirm with a face scan or PIN in the official app
Select the key file and type its password
Type a password, then a one-time code sent to the registered phone

scheme.mark_scheme: EDS – Select the key file and type its password; Password + SMS – Type a password, then a one-time code sent to the registered phone; eGov mobile – Confirm with a face scan or PIN in the official app.

questions.title: Advantages and risks
questions.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show whether the statement is an advantage or a risk of e-government.

prefill: Services are available 24 hours a day
Fake websites may steal citizens' passwords
Fewer face-to-face meetings with officials reduce corruption
Elderly people without Internet skills cannot use the services

scheme.mark_scheme: 1 Advantage (1); 2 Risk (1); 3 Advantage (1); 4 Risk (1)

questions.title: Using eGov safely
questions.text: Select **three** precautions a citizen should take when using eGov services.

options.content: Type egov.kz yourself or use the official app
Send the SMS code to anyone who says they are an official
Never share the EDS password
Log out after using a shared computer
Follow any link in an SMS about an unpaid fine

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C and D. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: A suspicious message
questions.text: Dana receives an SMS: *"Your eGov account will be blocked today. Confirm your data: http://egov-kz-check.top"*. What is this most likely to be?

options.content: An official notification from egov.kz
A phishing attack trying to steal her login data
A software update
A digital divide problem

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Unexpected urgency, a misspelled address and a link asking for data are signs of phishing.

questions.title: The digital divide
questions.text: Which is an example of the **digital divide** as a disadvantage of e-government?

options.content: Services are available 24/7
An elderly villager without Internet access or skills cannot use the online services
Less paperwork is needed
Applications can be tracked online

scheme.mark_scheme: B
scheme.explanation: Solutions include public service centres with assistants and training.

questions.title: If personal data leaks
questions.text: eGov holds citizens' IIN, address and family data. Select **two** problems that a leak of this data could cause.

options.content: Identity theft — loans taken out in someone else's name
Faster Internet speed for citizens
Fraud and harassment using the victims' addresses and phone numbers
Free certificates for everyone

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Protecting a game studio's work
questions.text: **Qazaq Pixel** is a small game studio in Shymkent. It has written a new adventure game, composed its soundtrack, invented a motion-sensing controller for the game and chosen the name and logo "Qazaq Pixel".

parts.title: Define intellectual property
parts.text: Define the term **intellectual property** and give **one** example from the studio.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- creations of the mind / intangible creations that the creator owns and has legal rights to control (1)
- an example from the stem: game code, soundtrack, controller design, name / logo (1)

points.criterion: Definition: creations of the mind owned by the creator

scheme.model_answer: Intellectual property is a creation of the mind, such as software or music, that its creator owns and has the legal right to control. Example: the source code of the adventure game.

parts.title: Which protection?
parts.text: Tick (✓) **one** box in each row to show how each item is protected.

prefill: The game's soundtrack
The motion-sensing controller
The name and logo "Qazaq Pixel"
The game's source code

scheme.mark_scheme: Soundtrack – Copyright (1); controller – Patent (1); name and logo – Trademark (1); source code – Copyright (1)
scheme.model_answer: Soundtrack: copyright. Controller: patent. Name and logo: trademark. Source code: copyright.

parts.title: Copyright and patent
parts.text: The studio did not apply for copyright on the game, but it must apply for a patent on the controller. Explain why.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- copyright arises automatically when an original work (the game) is created (1)
- a patent protects an invention and is only granted after an application / registration (1)

points.criterion: Patent must be applied for / registered for an invention

scheme.model_answer: Copyright protects the game automatically as soon as it is created, so no application is needed; the controller is an invention, and an invention is only protected by a patent after the studio applies for it and it is registered.

questions.title: Choosing software licences
questions.text: Qazaq Pixel sells the adventure game under a **proprietary** licence. It also wants to release a **level editor** that players can use to build their own levels, and a free **demo** of the game.

parts.title: Proprietary licence
parts.text: Describe **two** things the proprietary licence of the game does **not** allow a buyer to do.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any two (1 each):
- copy / share / sell copies to others
- install it on more devices than allowed
- see / change the source code / modify the program
- use it after the licence is cancelled / without paying
scheme.model_answer: A buyer may not give or sell copies of the game to other people, and may not see or change its source code.

parts.title: Freeware or open source
parts.text: The studio cannot decide whether to release the level editor as **freeware** or as **open source**. Explain the difference between the two.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- freeware: free to use but the source code is not available / cannot be modified (1)
- open source: the source code is available and can be studied, modified and shared (under the licence terms) (1)

points.criterion: Open source: code available, may modify

scheme.model_answer: Both are free, but freeware keeps the source code closed so users cannot change it, while open-source software publishes the source code so users may study, modify and share it under the licence.

parts.title: Advantage of open source
parts.text: Explain **one** advantage to the studio of releasing the level editor as open source.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- players / other developers can improve it, fix bugs or add features (1)
- so the editor gets better at no cost to the studio / builds a community / attracts more players to the game (1)
scheme.model_answer: Players and other programmers can fix bugs and add features to the editor themselves, so it improves at no cost to the studio and more people stay interested in the game.

parts.title: A free demo
parts.text: The demo can be played free for 7 days, then the full game must be bought. State the type of licence and explain why the studio uses it.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- shareware / trial (1)
- players can try the game before buying, which encourages them to pay / increases sales (1)

points.criterion: Reason: try before buying → more sales

scheme.model_answer: This is shareware (a trial licence). Players can try the game before paying, so more of them are convinced to buy the full version.

questions.title: Cracked copies of the game
questions.text: A month after release, "cracked" copies of Qazaq Pixel's game appear on a file-sharing site, and thousands of people download them.

scheme.mark_scheme: Copying / distributing / downloading / selling software without the permission of the copyright owner / without a licence (1)

points.criterion: Copying or sharing without permission / licence

scheme.model_answer: Software piracy is copying, sharing or downloading software without the permission of the copyright owner.

parts.title: Effect on the studio
parts.text: Analyse the effects of this piracy on the studio.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Up to 3 (1 each, a developed chain is needed for full marks):
- the studio loses sales / income from people who would have bought the game
- less money to pay staff / may have to cut jobs
- fewer updates / new games can be developed
- may need to spend money on legal action / anti-piracy measures
- may lose motivation / close down
scheme.model_answer: The studio loses income because many people play without buying the game. With less money it cannot pay all its developers, so it may cut staff, and it can produce fewer updates and new games.

parts.title: Risks for players
parts.text: Explain **two** risks for players who download a cracked copy.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any two (1 each):
- cracked copies often contain malware / viruses that can steal data
- no updates / patches / support
- legal risk: fines for breaking copyright law
- the game may not work / online features blocked
scheme.model_answer: The cracked file may contain malware that steals the player's passwords, and the player gets no updates or support and can be fined for breaking copyright law.

parts.title: Reducing piracy
parts.text: Suggest **two** methods the studio could use to reduce piracy of its next game.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any two (1 each):
- licence key / product activation / online account check
- DRM / copy protection
- legal action / ask the site to remove the copies (takedown)
- lower price / subscription / free demo so people buy legally
- educate players about the risks
scheme.model_answer: Require online activation with a licence key linked to the player's account, and ask the file-sharing site to remove the illegal copies (legal takedown).

questions.title: A school news website
questions.text: Grade 12 students run the school's news website. One student wants to copy an article about climate change from a news portal; another wants to publish a viral post claiming that "drinking hot water every hour protects against flu".

parts.title: Avoiding plagiarism
parts.text: Explain what **plagiarism** is and how the student could use the information in the article without plagiarising.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- plagiarism: presenting someone else's work / words / ideas as your own (without acknowledging the source) (1)
- rewrite in own words / quote in quotation marks and cite / reference the news portal (author, title, URL, date) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Plagiarism is presenting another person's work as your own. The student should summarise the article in their own words, put any exact sentences in quotation marks, and cite the news portal with the author, title, URL and date.

parts.title: Using photos legally
parts.text: State **two** ways the students can legally use photos on the website.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any two (1 each):
- use Creative Commons / copyright-free images and credit the author
- ask the owner for permission
- take their own photos
- buy a licence (stock photo)
scheme.model_answer: Use photos with a Creative Commons licence and credit the authors, or take their own photos.

parts.title: Problems of the viral post
parts.text: Analyse the problems that could be caused if the website publishes the post about hot water and flu.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any two linked points (1 each):
- readers may believe it and not see a doctor / not get vaccinated → their illness gets worse / spreads
- the school website loses trust / reputation; readers stop trusting reliable information
- it spreads further because readers share it
scheme.model_answer: Readers may rely on hot water instead of seeing a doctor, so they become more ill and infect others. When the claim is shown to be false, people stop trusting the school website and even reliable health advice.

parts.title: Checking before publishing
parts.text: Describe **two** checks the students should make before publishing a claim found online.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any two (1 each):
- check who published it / the author and whether the source is reliable / official
- compare with other reliable sources / official health sites / fact-checking sites
- check the date (is it current?)
- check whether it gives evidence or only emotion
scheme.model_answer: Check who published the claim and whether it is an official or expert source, and compare it with other reliable sources such as the Ministry of Health's website.

questions.title: Using egov.kz
questions.text: Aigerim, 18, needs a **certificate of no criminal record** for her university application. Her grandmother suggests going to a public service centre, but Aigerim decides to use **egov.kz**.

parts.title: Advantages of eGov
parts.text: Give **two** advantages to Aigerim of using egov.kz instead of visiting an office.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Any two (1 each):
- available 24/7 / from home / anywhere
- saves time — no travel or queues
- less paperwork — data filled in from state databases
- result quickly / can track the status
- less contact with officials / less corruption
scheme.model_answer: She can apply at any time from home without travelling, and she does not have to wait in a queue — the certificate arrives in her personal account within minutes.

parts.title: Steps to obtain the certificate
parts.text: Describe how Aigerim obtains the certificate through egov.kz.

scheme.mark_scheme:
Three steps in a sensible order (1 each):
- logs in to egov.kz / eGov mobile with an EDS or password + SMS code / biometrics
- chooses the service (certificate of no criminal record) and checks the automatically filled form
- signs the request with the EDS / SMS code
- receives the certificate (PDF with QR code) in her personal account / downloads it

points.criterion: Log in with EDS / SMS / app

scheme.model_answer: She logs in to egov.kz with her EDS, finds the certificate of no criminal record in the catalogue and checks the form that is filled in from state databases, signs the request with her EDS, and then downloads the certificate as a PDF with a QR code from her personal account.

parts.title: Purpose of the EDS
parts.text: Explain the purpose of the **electronic digital signature (EDS)** that Aigerim uses.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- confirms / proves the identity of the person signing (it is Aigerim) (1)
- shows the document has not been changed after signing / cannot be forged; has legal force (1)
scheme.model_answer: The EDS proves that the request really comes from Aigerim, and it shows that the signed document has not been changed after she signed it, so it has the same legal force as a handwritten signature.

parts.title: Responding to a suspicious SMS
parts.text: Next day Aigerim gets an SMS: *"Your eGov certificate is cancelled. Confirm your SMS code here: http://egov-kz.help"*. State **one** action she should take.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any one (1): do not follow the link / do not give the code / type egov.kz herself or use the official app to check / report or delete the message
scheme.model_answer: She should not open the link or send the code; she should check her account by typing egov.kz herself.

summary: Intellectual property and how it is protected (copyright, patents, trademarks, licences), the problems caused by disseminating and using information (piracy, plagiarism, misinformation, privacy breaches) and how to analyse them, and using e-government (eGov) resources of Kazakhstan safely.

blocks.content: Creations of the **mind** — inventions, software, books, music, films, designs, brand names and logos — that the **creator owns** and has the legal right to control, even though they are not physical objects.

The **legal right of the author** of an **original work** (program code, text, music, film, photo, website) to decide who may **copy, distribute, change or sell** it. It arises **automatically** when the work is created — no registration is needed.

A **registered right** that gives the inventor the **exclusive right to make, use and sell an invention** (a new technical solution, device or process) for a limited time (about **20 years**), in return for publishing how it works.
A **registered sign** — name, logo, slogan — that **identifies the products of one company** and distinguishes them from others (™ = claimed, ® = registered).

blocks.title: Ways intellectual property is protected
rows: **Original works**: software code, texts, music, films, photos, websites
**Automatically** when the work is created; lasts the author's life + 70 years (in Kazakhstan and many countries)
The code of a mobile game; a song
**Applied for** and registered; lasts about 20 years
**Brand names, logos, slogans** that identify a company's products
The logo of a Kazakh bank or airline

blocks.title: The law in Kazakhstan
blocks.content: The **Law on Copyright and Related Rights** protects works including **computer programs and databases**. Intellectual property is also protected by the **Civil Code**, and serious infringement is a criminal offence.

A **legal agreement** between the owner of the software and the user that states **how the software may be used** — on how many devices, whether it may be copied, shared or changed, and whether the source code is available.

blocks.title: Software licences
rows: Free for a **trial period**, then pay
Usually yes, but you may not change it
**Yes**, and you may **modify** it (under the licence terms, e.g. GPL)
Free, under conditions: attribution (BY), non-commercial (NC), no derivatives (ND), share-alike (SA)

theory.title: Problems caused by disseminating and using information

blocks.content: Digital information can be **copied and shared instantly, perfectly and almost free of charge**. This brings huge benefits, but also problems for creators, individuals and society.
**Copying, distributing, selling or downloading** software, films, music or books **without the permission** of the copyright owner (without a licence).
Presenting **someone else's work, words or ideas as your own** without acknowledging (citing) the source.
**Misinformation** is false or misleading information spread **by mistake**; **disinformation** is false information spread **deliberately** to deceive (fake news).

blocks.title: Problems of disseminating and using information
rows: Copying, sharing or selling software, films, music or books **without permission**
Creators and companies lose **income**; less money for new products; users risk **malware** in pirated copies
Presenting someone else's work or ideas **as your own** without acknowledging the source
The original author; the plagiarist's learning and reputation; academic honesty
Using images, music or videos in a website or video without a licence
Creators; the user may be **fined** or have content removed
False or misleading information spreads quickly on social media
Public **health**, elections, trust in media; people make wrong decisions
Personal information is published or shared without consent (doxxing, leaked databases)
False statements that damage someone's reputation
Too much information of mixed quality
Users find it hard to decide what is **true**

blocks.title: How to analyse a problem (exam answers)
items: **Name** the problem precisely (e.g. "plagiarism of a research project").
Say **what happens** — how the information is spread or used.
Say **who is harmed** — the creator, the user, other people, society.
Give the **consequence** for each (loss of income, malware, wrong decisions, loss of trust…).
Suggest a **solution or prevention** (licence, citation, fact-checking, consent).

items.title: Analysing a problem — piracy
items.content:
- **For the creator:** loss of sales and royalties; less money to pay developers.
- **For the user:** legal risk (fines), **no updates or support**, pirated copies often contain **malware**.
- **For society:** fewer new products, lower investment in the IT industry, lost tax revenue.
- **Ethically:** it is using someone else's work **without paying** for it.
- **Prevention:** licence keys and online activation, copy protection (DRM), legal action to remove illegal copies, affordable prices / subscriptions and free demos.

items.title: Analysing a problem — fake news
items.content:
- Spreads **faster** than corrections because it is shocking or emotional.
- Can cause **panic**, damage reputations, influence **elections** or harm health (false cures).
- Makes people **distrust** all media, including reliable sources.
- **Solutions:** check the source, compare with other reliable sources, look at the date, use fact-checking sites, think before sharing.

blocks.title: How to use information legally and ethically
rows: Using a photo from the Internet in a project
Use **copyright-free / Creative Commons** images and **credit** the author, or ask permission
Quoting a book or website in an essay
Use **quotation marks** and **cite the source** (author, title, date, URL)
Buy a **licence** or use **free / open-source** alternatives
**Check** that it comes from a reliable source before sharing
Get their **consent**; do not share personal data

blocks.title: Worked example — a school documentary
blocks.content:
Students of grade 12 make a video about Almaty for a competition. They plan to use (1) a popular song, (2) photos found with a search engine, (3) a paragraph copied from a travel website.
- **Song:** protected by copyright → use **royalty-free / Creative Commons** music or ask the rights holder; otherwise the video may be removed and the school fined.
- **Photos:** search-engine results are **not** free to use → filter by **Creative Commons** licence and **credit** each author, or take their own photos.
- **Text:** copying it without credit is **plagiarism** → write it in their own words and **cite** the website, or quote it in quotation marks with the source.

blocks.title: Fair use / exceptions
blocks.content: Copyright law allows limited use without permission for **education, criticism, news reporting and quotation**, as long as the source is acknowledged and only a **reasonable part** is used.

theory.title: Exam practice: intellectual property and information problems

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Define the term intellectual property. [1]**
Creations of the mind (inventions, software, texts, music, designs, logos) that the creator owns and has legal rights over (1).

**Q: Explain the difference between copyright and a patent. [2]**
Copyright protects **original works** such as software code and texts and is **automatic** (1); a patent protects an **invention** and must be **applied for and registered** (1).

**Q: Analyse one problem that arises when software is copied illegally. [3]**
The developer **loses income** from sales (1), so it has less money to employ programmers and develop updates or new products (1); users of pirated copies risk **malware** and get no support or updates (1).

**Q: Explain the difference between freeware and open-source software. [2]**
Freeware is free to use but the **source code is not available / cannot be changed** (1); open-source software makes the **source code available and allows it to be modified** and shared (1).

**Q: State two ways a student can avoid plagiarism. [2]**
Cite / reference every source (author, title, URL, date) (1); put ideas in their own words / use quotation marks for exact quotes (1).

- Writing "it is illegal" as the only problem of piracy — **analyse**: who loses what, and why.
- Mixing up plagiarism (claiming authorship) and piracy (copying without a licence).
- Writing "check the information" — say **how**: the source, other reliable sources, the date.

blocks.title: Check yourself
items: What is intellectual property? Name four ways to protect it and what each protects.
Which protection is automatic, and which must be registered?
Compare proprietary, shareware, freeware and open-source licences.
Analyse the effects of piracy on creators, users and society.
How can you check whether a news story is fake?
How should you use images and quotations from the Internet in a project?

blocks.content: The use of the **Internet and digital technologies** by the state to provide **public services** to citizens and businesses **online**. In Kazakhstan the main portal is **egov.kz** with the **eGov mobile** app.

A service provided by a state body to a citizen or business — a certificate, a registration, a payment, an application — which can be **requested and received through the eGov portal** without visiting an office.

blocks.title: Examples of eGov services in Kazakhstan
columns: What the citizen can do online
rows: Get a certificate of address registration, no criminal record, birth or marriage certificate
Register a place of residence, a car, a business (individual entrepreneur)
Apply to a kindergarten or school, see UNT results, apply for grants
Attach to a clinic, book a doctor's appointment
Apply for benefits and pensions, check pension savings (ENPF)
Show an ID card or driving licence from the phone instead of the paper document

blocks.title: Worked example — a certificate for a school application
blocks.content:
Mr Seitkali needs a **certificate of address registration** for his son's school application.
1. He opens **egov.kz** (typing the address himself) or the **eGov mobile** app and logs in with his **EDS** (or password + one-time SMS code).
2. He finds *Certificate of address registration* in the service catalogue.
3. His name, IIN and address are **filled in automatically** from the state databases; he checks them.
4. He **signs** the request with his EDS / SMS code.
5. A few minutes later the certificate appears as a **PDF with a QR code** in his personal account; the school can check it by scanning the QR code.
He saved a trip to a public service centre and a queue — and paid nothing.

blocks.title: Advantages and disadvantages of e-government
rows: Needs **Internet access**, a device and digital skills — the **digital divide** (elderly, rural areas)
Risk of **cyber-attacks** and leaks of citizens' personal data
**Less paperwork**; documents checked automatically between databases
**Phishing** — fake eGov sites and SMS messages that steal passwords or EDS
**Less corruption** — fewer face-to-face contacts with officials
**Transparent** — the citizen can track the status of an application
People may lose or share their EDS key and password

theory.title: Using eGov safely: digital signature and security

blocks.content: A **cryptographic key pair** (a private key kept by the owner, protected by a password, and a public certificate issued by the National Certification Authority) used to **sign electronic documents**. It **proves who signed** the document and **shows that it has not been changed** after signing; it has the same legal force as a handwritten signature.

blocks.caption: Real portal or phishing copy?

blocks.content:
- Type **egov.kz** yourself or use the official app — do not follow links in unexpected messages.
- **Never share** your EDS password or SMS codes with anyone (officials never ask for them).
- Keep the EDS file on a protected device and **log out** on shared computers.
- Check that the site uses **HTTPS** and the correct address.
- Do not let other people sign documents with **your** EDS — whatever is signed with it is legally yours.

items.title: Personal data on eGov
items.content:
- The portal holds **sensitive personal data** — IIN, address, family, income, health records.
- A leak can lead to **identity theft**, fraud (loans taken in someone's name) and loss of privacy.
- Citizens should **check** the notifications about who requested their data, and report anything unusual.

items.title: Who is left behind?
items.content:
- The **digital divide**: elderly people, people in remote villages, people without smartphones.
- Solutions: **public service centres (ЦОН)** with assistants, self-service terminals, training courses, simple mobile apps.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Describe what is meant by e-government. [2]**
The state uses the Internet / digital technology (1) to provide public services to citizens and businesses online, e.g. egov.kz (1).

**Q: Give two advantages of using e-government services. [2]**
Services are available **24/7** without visiting an office (1); **saves time** / no queues / less paperwork / less corruption (1).

**Q: Explain the purpose of an electronic digital signature. [2]**
It **confirms the identity** of the person signing (1) and shows that the document **has not been changed** after it was signed (1).

**Q: Describe how a citizen receives a certificate through egov.kz. [3]**
Logs in with an EDS / password + SMS (1); chooses the service and checks the automatically filled form (1); signs the request and receives the certificate (PDF with QR code) in the personal account (1).

**Q: Explain one risk of e-government and how to reduce it. [2]**
Phishing — fake sites / messages steal the EDS password or SMS code (1); type the address yourself / use the official app and never share codes (1).

- Listing eGov services without saying what the **benefit** is.
- Thinking an EDS is a picture of your handwritten signature — it is a **cryptographic key**.
- Giving "hackers" as a risk without saying **what** can happen (leak of personal data, identity theft).
- Forgetting the **digital divide** when evaluating e-government.
